U0001.d: U0001 is the umbrella code for trouble on the high-speed CAN, the fast two-wire network joining engine, transmission, brake and steering modules. GM/Saab logs it once a module's transmit error counter climbs past 255: that module disconnects itself, stops sending and works with substitute values.
s: Several warning lamps and messages at the same time
Scan tool reaches some modules only or none at all
Shifting, steering assist or brake functions in fallback mode
Many lost-communication codes stored alongside
c: Bus pair chafed, pinched or crushed in the harness
Corroded, loose or bent pins at a module or splice connector
One module or its transceiver disturbing the whole bus
History entry after a voltage dip or tester connected with ignition on

U0002.d: U0002 stands for impaired rather than lost traffic on the high-speed CAN, and makers fill the slot in different ways. GM/Saab sets it when a supervised periodic message, which also tells the receiver that its sender is alive, has not shown up within the 250 ms supervision time; the receiver then carries on with a default value.
s: Warning lamps that appear and disappear again
Single functions briefly unavailable
Code stored as history without a current fault
c: Intermittent contact at connectors or splices of the bus pair
Module software reacting to short voltage dips (reflash available)
Weak battery or poor ground causing brief module resets
Electrical interference from retrofitted devices on the bus

U0003.d: U0003 reports a break in the (+) wire of the high-speed CAN, which GM and FCA also call CAN-High. At rest this line idles near 2.5 V and is lifted about one volt for each dominant bit.
s: Modules beyond the break no longer reachable
Several warnings and fallback modes at once
Fault appears or disappears when the harness is moved
c: CAN-High conductor broken at a flex point or after a repair
CAN-High terminal pushed back or corroded in a connector
Diagnostic interface connected with ignition on (history code only)

U0004.d: U0004 means the (+) wire of the high-speed CAN, CAN-High, is dragged below its valid range, usually by a short to ground. This is one of the faults the physical layer cannot absorb: a sending node is unable to produce a dominant bit, every frame attempt fails, the error counters rise and the controllers end up bus-off, as onsemi's bench measurements show.
s: Network-wide communication loss, scan tool cannot connect
Engine, gearbox, ABS and steering warnings together
Vehicle may not start or run in limp mode
c: CAN-High insulation damaged and touching body ground
Harness clamped by a screw, bracket or seat rail
Defective transceiver in one module pulling CAN-High down

U0005.d: U0005 flags CAN-High, the (+) wire of the high-speed bus, sitting above its permitted range, generally because it touches battery voltage or a 5 V feed. Unlike a ground short this does not have to halt traffic: onsemi and NXP both found that frames still pass, but the voltage picture is distorted, noise immunity worsens and, on networks with a large capacitive load, bit timing can be violated.
s: Sporadic warnings, often with no lasting malfunction
Individual messages or modules dropping out under load or in damp weather
c: CAN-High chafed through against a battery or ignition feed
Moisture bridging CAN-High to a supply pin in a connector
Incorrectly connected accessory or retrofit module

U0006.d: U0006 points to an interrupted CAN-Low conductor, i.e. the (-) line on the high-speed network.
s: Part of the modules unreachable, others still respond
Warnings from the affected systems, sometimes only when moving doors or harness
c: CAN-Low conductor fractured at a hinge or flex point
Corroded splice or connector in the CAN-Low path
CAN-Low terminal backed out after work on the harness

U0007.d: U0007 reports that the (-) line CAN-Low on the fast bus is held below its valid band, normally by a short to ground. The physical layer copes with this particular case: onsemi recorded ongoing transmission with a distorted level pattern and raised transceiver current, and NXP counts it among the hidden failures.
s: Usually no noticeable malfunction, code found during a scan
Occasional short-lived warnings, worse with moisture
c: CAN-Low insulation worn through against body metal
Water in a connector bridging CAN-Low to a ground pin
Module transceiver internally shorted on its CAN-Low pin

U0008.d: U0008 means CAN-Low, the (-) wire of the high-speed CAN, is forced too high, typically through contact with the 12 V system or another supply rail. This fault blocks the bus: CAN-Low can no longer be driven down, no dominant state develops, and both onsemi and NXP found that transmission becomes impossible.
s: Total communication loss on the high-speed network
Many warning lamps, possible no-start
Scan tool cannot reach powertrain modules
c: CAN-Low chafed against a battery or ignition supply wire
Retrofit wiring tapped into the bus pair by mistake
Bent pin or moisture linking CAN-Low to a supply contact

U0009.d: U0009 describes CAN-Low and CAN-High of the high-speed bus being shorted to each other. The voltage difference between them then stays at zero, which every receiver interprets as recessive, so a dominant bit can never form; onsemi's tests show transmission stopping entirely and controllers running into bus-off.
s: No communication on the high-speed network at all
Numerous warnings, fallback modes, possibly no start
Scan tool reaches only modules on other networks
c: Bus pair crushed so that both conductors touch
Water or corrosion bridging CAN-High and CAN-Low in a splice or connector
Failed transceiver shorting both bus pins inside a module

U0010.d: U0010 is the general fault code for the medium-speed CAN, a slower two-wire network that several makers run next to the fast powertrain bus. Saab/GM documents it as mid-speed GMLAN with (+) and (-) wires and a terminating resistor across them, Ford as MS-CAN; on the F-Super Duty an unplugged connector C408 interrupts it and takes climate control, front control panel and headlamp logic down with it.
s: Climate control, lighting or infotainment functions inoperative
Several body modules unreachable with the scan tool
On heavy trucks MIL and engine derate possible
c: Connector in the medium-speed network unplugged or not seated
Harness chafed or wet at doors, tailgate or body mounts
Residual code after module replacement or programming

U0011.d: U0011 says the medium-speed CAN is running but not dependably: expected periodic messages come late or not at all, error frames accumulate, or a node briefly goes bus-off and rejoins. No manufacturer publicly documents U0011 in its J2012 sense with thresholds.
s: Comfort functions such as windows, locks or climate controls work intermittently
Code stored as history in body modules
c: Loose or corroded connector on the medium-speed pair
Low battery voltage or poor ground causing module resets
Module software miscounting or missing messages (update needed)

U0012.d: U0012 reports an interruption of CAN-High, the (+) wire of the medium-speed CAN. Saab's mid-speed GMLAN uses the same two-wire layout as the fast bus, with a terminating resistor between (+) and (-), so a break isolates the modules downstream and alters the resistance seen between the lines.
s: Comfort and body modules behind the break inoperative
Climate, lighting or switch panel functions missing
c: Body or upfitter connector in the medium-speed (+) path left open
CAN-High conductor broken in a door or tailgate harness

U0013.d: U0013 indicates that CAN-High on the medium-speed bus, the (+) wire, is pulled toward ground. Where this network uses the same differential layout as high-speed CAN, as Saab's terminated mid-speed GMLAN suggests, a grounded CAN-High rules out any dominant bit; onsemi and NXP list this short among those that end all communication.
s: All comfort and infotainment modules fail together
Engine and transmission keep working normally
c: Medium-speed CAN-High insulation damaged against body ground
Wires broken open in a door boot or tailgate grommet
Comfort module transceiver pulling CAN-High down

U0014.d: U0014 means CAN-High of the medium-speed bus lies above its normal range, most often because the (+) wire touches battery voltage. On a differential CAN of the high-speed type this is a fault the network rides through: onsemi and NXP found frames still being delivered, but with shifted levels, reduced noise margin and higher current draw in the transceivers.
s: Occasional unresponsive switches or flickering displays
Stored code without obvious malfunction
c: Medium-speed CAN-High rubbing against a supply wire
Moisture in a door or roof connector linking CAN-High to plus
Aftermarket device wired to the comfort bus incorrectly

U0015.d: U0015 stands for a break in CAN-Low, the (-) conductor of the medium-speed CAN. Modules separated by the break stop exchanging data with the rest of the network, whereas units still connected on both wires keep working; which functions disappear therefore depends on where the line is cut.
s: Only some comfort functions lost, depending on break location
Fault varies when doors or seats are moved
c: CAN-Low conductor fractured in a moving harness section
Connector not reconnected after body or upfit work

U0016.d: U0016 reports CAN-Low of the medium-speed bus, the (-) wire, sitting below its valid range, typically through a short to ground. Transferred from the high-speed physical layer, which Saab's two-wire terminated mid-speed GMLAN resembles, this is a fault the bus tolerates: onsemi measured continuing transmission with deformed levels, and NXP files it as a hidden failure visible only to transceivers with diagnosis.
s: Usually no lasting malfunction, code found during a scan
Sporadic glitches in comfort functions
c: Medium-speed CAN-Low chafed against a ground point or sheet edge
Water ingress in a footwell or door connector
Comfort module transceiver internally shorted on CAN-Low

U0017.d: U0017 means CAN-Low on the medium-speed CAN, the (-) wire, is held too high, as a rule by contact with battery or another supply voltage. On a differential bus of the high-speed type this short is fatal for traffic: the line cannot be pulled down, no dominant bit appears, and onsemi and NXP both class it among the shorts that make transmission impossible.
s: All comfort and infotainment modules out at once
Climate, locking or radio not responding
c: Medium-speed CAN-Low chafed against a supply wire
Moisture or bent pin linking CAN-Low to a supply contact
Accessory wiring connected to the comfort bus by mistake

U0018.d: U0018 describes the two medium-speed CAN lines, CAN-Low and CAN-High, shorted together. With no voltage difference left, receivers see only recessive bits, nobody can win arbitration, and the controllers on the segment eventually go bus-off; onsemi's measurements on the comparable high-speed layer show transmission stopping completely.
s: Entire comfort network fails, powertrain unaffected
Body modules unreachable with the scan tool
c: Medium-speed bus pair crushed so both wires touch
Water in a connector bridging (+) and (-)
Failed transceiver shorting both bus pins in a comfort module

U0019.d: U0019 is the general fault slot for the low-speed CAN, the slow body network serving doors, lighting, locks and comfort electronics. Two physical forms exist: the two-wire fault-tolerant CAN of ISO 11898-3, which NXP's TJA1055 runs at up to 125 kBd and keeps alive on one wire after a single break or short, and the one-conductor low-speed GMLAN that GM runs at 33.33 kbit/s.
s: Comfort functions such as locks, lighting or windows fail or act erratically
Anti-theft alarm triggers without obvious reason
Lost-communication codes for several body modules
MIL on in some vehicles (FCA ProMaster 2015)
c: Damaged low-speed bus wiring or corroded, loose connector pins
Poor supply or ground at a module on the body bus
Module software logging the code without a real fault (FCA ProMaster BCM)
Faulty module or transceiver disturbing the low-speed bus

U0020.d: U0020 reports a low-speed CAN that still runs but delivers its traffic unreliably. GM documents it for the 2011 Saab 9-5, whose low-speed GMLAN is a single wire: a module sets U0020 when a monitored cyclic message, which doubles as proof that the sender is available, fails to arrive, and then substitutes a default value.
s: Often no noticeable symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts of comfort or display functions
Several modules store communication codes at the same time
c: Code stored while modules wake up or after the supply was interrupted
Software anomaly in one module (GM video processing module 2019)
Gateway module stops communicating or has loose terminals
Intermittent contact in the low-speed bus wiring

U0021.d: U0021 marks a break in the (+) wire of a two-wire low-speed CAN, called CAN-High in the fault-tolerant layout of ISO 11898-3. There the wire rests close to 0 V and is pulled toward 5 V for a dominant bit, the reverse of the high-speed pattern.
s: Usually no noticeable effect, the bus keeps running
Occasional comfort function glitches, especially with interference
Code stored only in modules on one side of the break
c: CAN-High wire broken at a flex point such as a door transition
Pushed-back or spread terminal in a connector
Corrosion in a connector or splice

U0022.d: U0022 indicates a ground short on CAN-High, the positive conductor of a dual-wire low-speed CAN. In the fault-tolerant design of ISO 11898-3, where CAN-High idles at about 0 V and only rises for dominant bits, a ground short simply takes that rise away.
s: Frequently no symptom besides the stored code
Rare sporadic comfort function faults
c: CAN-High insulation chafed through against body ground
Wire pierced by a trim screw or trapped under a seat rail
Internal transceiver fault pulling CAN-High low

U0023.d: U0023 means CAN-High, the (+) conductor of a dual-line low-speed CAN, sits too high, typically shorted to battery voltage or a 5 V supply. Under ISO 11898-3 this pins the line at a level the receivers read as permanently dominant.
s: Comfort functions mostly still work, occasional glitches
Increased sensitivity to interference, e.g. with radio transmitters nearby
Code stored in several body modules
c: CAN-High chafed against a battery feed or ignition wire
Water in a connector bridging CAN-High to a supply pin
Retrofitted accessory tapped into the wrong wire

U0024.d: U0024 reports an interruption of the (-) line, CAN-Low, of a two-wire low-speed CAN. Under the ISO 11898-3 fault-tolerant scheme this wire idles near 5 V and is pulled toward ground for dominant bits.
s: Typically no symptom, code found during a scan
Comfort functions behind the break react sluggishly or sporadically
c: CAN-Low wire broken in a door or tailgate harness
CAN-Low terminal backed out of its connector
Corroded CAN-Low contact after water entry

U0025.d: U0025 flags CAN-Low pulled toward ground on a low-speed CAN with two conductors. In the fault-tolerant physical layer of ISO 11898-3 CAN-Low idles near 5 V, so a ground short forces it into its dominant state for good.
s: Comfort functions work but drop out now and then
Body modules store the code repeatedly
c: CAN-Low insulation damaged and touching body ground
Harness trapped by a panel, bracket or seat mechanism
Module transceiver internally shorting CAN-Low to ground

U0026.d: U0026 means CAN-Low, the (-) line of a two-wire low-speed CAN, is held too high. Since this wire already sits near 5 V at rest in an ISO 11898-3 network, the outcome depends on where the short goes.
s: Often no noticeable effect
Occasional comfort function dropouts when the bus runs on one wire
c: CAN-Low chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Moisture in a connector linking CAN-Low to a supply pin
Faulty transceiver driving CAN-Low to its supply

U0027.d: U0027 describes the two wires of a low-speed CAN, (+) and (-), touching each other. On a high-speed bus such a short ends all traffic, but the fault-tolerant layer of ISO 11898-3 is built to ride it out.
s: Comfort network keeps running, sometimes with dropouts
Higher sensitivity to electrical interference
Code stored in several body modules at once
c: Harness crushed so that both bus wires make contact
Water in a splice or connector bridging the two wires
Damaged transceiver bridging its two bus pins

U0028.d: U0028 is the general code for Vehicle Communication Bus A, a neutral label each maker assigns to a network of its choosing. GM uses it in the radio of many 2013-19 models as the health indicator of the MOST infotainment ring, which the radio masters: a current U0028 symptom 00 points to a MOST module with a power, ground or wake-up fault, found by bypassing modules with kit EL-51578 until the code turns to history.
s: Infotainment functions dead: blank radio display, no audio, steering wheel controls inoperative (GM)
Battery or electrical system warning in the cluster (Audi mild hybrid)
Several warning lamps, vehicle may not be drivable (Audi Q5 PHEV)
Further communication codes stored alongside
c: Power, ground or wake-up fault at a module on the bus (GM MOST ring)
Bus or supply wiring chafed or pinched (Audi Q5 PHEV, GM dash harness)
Connectors not fully seated or locked, spread pins
Wrong module configuration or software fault (Isuzu FMS, GM brake module 2026)

U0029.d: U0029 reports that Vehicle Communication Bus A works, but not reliably; which network that is depends on the maker. In Audi's 48 V mild hybrids (A6 up to Q8, 2019-23) the engine control unit logs U002900 for its sensor/hybrid CAN, labelled there as no communication, together with U002800; the belt starter-generator is then set to freewheel, the battery is no longer charged and a yellow or red battery warning appears.
s: Yellow or red battery warning, battery not charging (Audi mild hybrid)
Intermittent warning messages from several systems
Comfort or infotainment functions drop out briefly
c: Connector not fully seated or locked, spread or bent pins
Harness chafed on underbody trim or pinched at a dash bracket
Faulty sensor on the bus disturbing communication (Audi brake servo pressure sensor)
Gateway module stops communicating until reset

U0030.d: U0030 stands for an open circuit in the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus A. What that wire is depends on the network a maker assigns to Bus A; where it is a two-wire CAN, like the sensor/hybrid CAN Audi files under this name in its 48 V mild hybrids, the (+) line is CAN-High.
s: Functions served by modules beyond the break stop working
Lost-communication codes for some modules on Bus A
c: (+) wire of Bus A broken in the harness
Terminal backed out or spread in a connector
Connector left unplugged after a repair

U0031.d: U0031 indicates a ground short on the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus A. Where Bus A is a high-speed-style two-wire CAN, such as the sensor/hybrid CAN Audi assigns to this slot in its 48 V mild hybrids, the (+) wire is CAN-High, which has to rise by about a volt to form a dominant bit.
s: All functions served by Bus A fail at once
Many lost-communication codes in other modules
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the modules involved
c: (+) wire chafed through against body ground
Harness trapped under a panel or bracket
Transceiver of one module shorting the (+) line internally

U0032.d: U0032 reports excess voltage on the (+) line of Vehicle Communication Bus A, usually from contact with battery voltage. If Bus A is a two-wire CAN of the high-speed type, as Audi's sensor/hybrid CAN, the (+) wire is CAN-High.
s: Sporadic warnings or brief function dropouts
Only one module reports the fault, vehicle otherwise normal
c: (+) wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector bridging the (+) wire to a supply pin
Aftermarket device connected to the bus wire

U0033.d: U0033 reports an interruption of the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus A; on a dual-line CAN like the sensor/hybrid CAN Audi lists as Bus A, that is CAN-Low. As with U0030, the network falls apart into pieces that can no longer hear each other, and NXP stresses that a standard high-speed transceiver has no means of detecting an open wire on its own.
s: Modules beyond the break stop responding
Lost-communication codes stored alongside
c: (-) wire of Bus A broken in the harness
Pushed-back or corroded terminal in a connector
Connector not reconnected after a repair

U0034.d: U0034 flags the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus A pulled toward ground. On a high-speed-type CAN, the layout Audi uses for the sensor/hybrid CAN behind this slot, that wire is CAN-Low, which normally drops by about a volt for dominant bits.
s: Intermittent communication errors, vehicle mostly normal
Code reported by a single module
c: (-) wire insulation damaged and touching ground
Harness pinched by a bracket or panel
Faulty transceiver pulling the (-) line to ground

U0035.d: U0035 means the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus A is held too high, typically shorted to battery voltage. On a two-wire high-speed-type CAN, such as Audi's sensor/hybrid CAN filed under Bus A, this is CAN-Low.
s: All functions on Bus A fail together
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the modules involved
c: (-) wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector linking the (-) wire to a supply pin
Damaged transceiver driving the (-) line high

U0036.d: U0036 describes a short between the (+) and (-) wires of Vehicle Communication Bus A. On a CAN-type bus the differential voltage then stays at zero, receivers see only recessive bits and, as onsemi's measurements on high-speed CAN show, no frame can be sent any more; NXP adds that transceiver diagnosis cannot detect this short.
s: Several warning lamps on at once
Vehicle may refuse to drive (Audi Q5 PHEV)
Drive-motor and power-electronics codes stored alongside
c: Harness chafed so that both bus wires touch (Audi Q5 PHEV: underbody trim)
Water in a splice or connector bridging the two wires
Damaged transceiver shorting its bus pins

U0037.d: U0037 is the umbrella code for Vehicle Communication Bus B, the second neutral network slot after Bus A; each maker decides which network sits behind it, and published uses differ widely. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg data book sets it when a CAN frame sent on Bus B goes unacknowledged.
s: Warning lamps of the systems on Bus B, e.g. ABS lamp (Jeep) or check-engine lamp (Volvo)
Stop/start or chassis functions unavailable
Lost-communication codes stored alongside
c: Loose or corroded ground or supply of a module on Bus B (FCA: ground G907A)
Module software misreporting or mishandling the bus (Volvo BCM2, Ford VDM, GM brake module 2026)
Damaged bus wiring or a poorly seated connector
A module on Bus B that has stopped answering

U0038.d: U0038 flags Vehicle Communication Bus B as present but unreliable: frames arrive late, incompletely or for a while not at all, rather than the bus being dead outright. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg data book describes the trigger as a global time-out in which no messages come in any longer.
s: Selector stuck in Park, engine does not crank (Honda Civic CVT)
Several warning lamps on at once
Functions drop out intermittently
c: Internal fault in a module on Bus B (Honda Civic: transmission control module)
Loose or corroded terminals interrupting traffic now and then
Software mismatch between modules on the bus

U0039.d: U0039 reports a break in the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus B, which on a CAN-type network is CAN-High. Deutz assigns this code to the third CAN channel of its EMR L1 engine controller and lists it for main and secondary ECU simply as an open circuit on CAN 3, without naming the wire.
s: Functions of modules beyond the break unavailable
Lost-communication codes for individual modules
c: (+) wire of Bus B broken, often at a flex point
Terminal backed out or spread in a connector
Connector left open after repair work

U0040.d: U0040 indicates the (+) line of Vehicle Communication Bus B pulled down to ground potential. On a high-speed-type CAN that is CAN-High, and onsemi's bench tests list it among the shorts that stop all transmission: each failed start of frame raises the transmit error counter by eight, the controller turns error passive after a handful of attempts and goes bus-off once the count passes 255.
s: All functions on Bus B fail at once (high-speed type)
Many lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Fallback modes or warning lamps depending on the modules involved
c: (+) wire chafed through against body ground
Harness crushed by a seat rail, bracket or panel
Transceiver of one module pulling the (+) line to ground

U0041.d: U0041 means the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus B sits at too high a voltage, typically because it touches a battery or 5 V supply. For a high-speed-type CAN this is CAN-High, and NXP classes a short of CAN-High to battery or to VCC as a hidden failure: frames keep flowing, so only a transceiver with bus diagnosis, such as the TJA1043, reports it.
s: Often no noticeable symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic warnings from one module
c: (+) wire chafed against a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector bridging the (+) wire to a supply pin
Faulty transceiver driving the (+) line high

U0042.d: U0042 points to an interrupted (-) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus B; on a CAN-type bus that is CAN-Low. The network then splits along the break, and on a standard high-speed CAN neither side's transceiver can tell what happened, since NXP states that line interruptions escape even transceiver diagnosis.
s: Modules beyond the break no longer respond
Lost-communication codes stored alongside
c: (-) wire of Bus B broken in the harness
Corroded or pushed-back terminal in a connector
Connector not reconnected after a repair

U0043.d: U0043 reports the (-) line of Vehicle Communication Bus B shorted toward ground. Where Bus B is built like a high-speed CAN, that line is CAN-Low, and the fault is sneaky: onsemi measured frames still getting through, with distorted levels and the node drawing about 72 mA instead of 65 mA, because the CANH driver now pushes current through the termination into ground.
s: Vehicle mostly normal, code stored by a single module
Occasional communication errors
c: (-) wire insulation damaged and touching ground
Harness trapped under a panel or bracket
Faulty transceiver pulling the (-) line to ground

U0044.d: U0044 means the (-) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus B is held at an excessive voltage, mostly through contact with battery plus. Where Bus B is a high-speed-type CAN, the conductor is CAN-Low, and onsemi found that with CAN-Low at 12 V no frame gets out any more; the node's current even drops, to about 48 mA, because its transmit pin is driven low only some 2 % of the time while the controller retries and back
s: All functions on Bus B fail together (high-speed type)
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Fallback modes or warning lamps depending on the modules involved
c: (-) wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector linking the (-) wire to a supply pin
Damaged transceiver driving the (-) line high

U0045.d: U0045 describes the two wires of Vehicle Communication Bus B touching each other. Deutz uses this code in the EMR L1 engine controller for a short circuit on its third CAN channel, without further detail.
s: Every function on Bus B unavailable (high-speed type)
Several warning lamps on at once
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
c: Harness crushed so that both bus wires touch
Water in a splice or connector bridging the two wires
Damaged module input shorting its bus pins

U0046.d: U0046 covers Vehicle Communication Bus C in general, the third manufacturer-assigned network slot after Bus A and Bus B. Public uses are rare.
s: Check-engine lamp possible together with other stored codes (Ram 1500)
Functions of modules on Bus C unavailable
Lost-communication codes stored alongside
c: Control module software that misjudges the bus (Ram 1500: PCM flash)
Damaged bus wiring or poorly seated connector on Bus C
Supply or ground fault at a module on Bus C

U0047.d: U0047 says that Vehicle Communication Bus C is up but its traffic is not dependable, for instance through sporadic error frames, messages arriving too late or brief dropouts. CAN controllers keep score with error counters: as onsemi explains with reference to ISO 11898-1, every failed transmission adds eight to the transmit counter, beyond about 128 the node turns error passive and past 255 it takes itself off the bu
s: Functions drop out briefly and return
Sporadic warning messages from several systems
c: Loose or corroded terminals on Bus C
A module on Bus C resetting because of weak supply or ground
Interference coupled into the bus wiring

U0048.d: U0048 stands for an open (+) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus C, CAN-High where Bus C is a CAN. Deutz places the code on CAN 4 of its EMR L1 engine controller, listed for main and secondary ECU as an open circuit on that channel, just as U0039 covers CAN 3.
s: Modules on the far side of the break unreachable
Lost-communication codes in several modules
c: (+) wire of Bus C broken at a flex point or splice

U0049.d: U0049 reports the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus C shorted to ground. If Bus C is a high-speed-type CAN, the affected conductor is CAN-High; for a dominant bit it should climb to roughly 3.6 V, which a grounded line cannot do, and onsemi's tests show the node unable to send anything while its CANH output works into a current limit of up to about 120 mA.
s: All functions on Bus C fail together (high-speed type)
Missing-message codes in modules on other networks
c: (+) wire of Bus C chafed through to ground
Harness pinched during assembly or repair
Shorted transceiver in a module on Bus C

U0050.d: U0050 flags excess voltage on the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus C. On a high-speed-style CAN bus, the conductor is CAN-High sitting at battery or 5 V level, a condition onsemi found survivable: frames still pass, the dominant bits merely look different and the transceiver draws about as little as when idle, since its high-side driver delivers no current.
s: Usually no symptom, code found during a scan
Occasional single warning from a module on Bus C
c: (+) wire of Bus C touching a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector linking the bus wire to supply
Aftermarket device tapped into the bus wire

U0051.d: U0051 stands for a severed (-) conductor on Vehicle Communication Bus C, CAN-Low where Bus C is a CAN. Deutz, which places Bus C on the fourth CAN channel of the EMR L1 engine control unit, does not use this code and books CAN 4 faults only as open circuit (U0048) or short circuit (U0054).
s: Modules beyond the break no longer respond
Code comes and goes while other modules keep working
c: (-) wire of Bus C broken at a flex point or splice
Terminal pushed back or spread in a Bus C connector

U0052.d: U0052 signals a ground short on the (-) line of Vehicle Communication Bus C; where Bus C follows the high-speed CAN layout, the affected line is CAN-Low, and NXP's application note for the TJA1041 lists this short among the hidden bus failures: nodes keep communicating, so a controller only learns of it from a transceiver with bus diagnosis. Such a transceiver needs at least four dominant phases of 4 µs or more on th
s: Often no noticeable symptom, code found during a scan
Occasional brief warning from a module on Bus C
c: (-) wire of Bus C chafed against body metal
Harness trapped under a trim panel or seat rail
Transceiver in one module pulling CAN-Low to ground

U0053.d: U0053 reports too much voltage on the (-) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus C, meaning CAN-Low if Bus C is built as a high-speed CAN, and NXP's TJA1041 application note states that a short of CAN-Low either to battery or to the 5 V transceiver supply makes communication impossible, while onsemi's measurements show the transmitting node stuck in endless failed attempts. All Bus C members go quiet together.
s: All functions on Bus C drop out at once (high-speed type)
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the affected modules
c: (-) wire of Bus C touching a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector bridging the (-) wire to a supply pin

U0054.d: U0054 describes a short between the two wires of Vehicle Communication Bus C. Deutz uses it in main and secondary EMR L1 engine controllers as a short circuit on CAN 4, the same channel whose open circuit is U0048.
s: All modules on Bus C unreachable (high-speed type)
Engine controller reports CAN fault, connected machine functions fail (Deutz)
c: Harness crushed so that both Bus C wires touch
Water in a splice or connector bridging the pair
Damaged module input shorting its two bus pins

U0055.d: U0055 covers Vehicle Communication Bus D as a whole, the fourth network slot a manufacturer can assign freely. Volvo documents it for the 2016-17 XC90 T8 plug-in hybrid: the engine control module stores U005500 with fault type intermittent, the driver information display shows the turtle symbol and the car lacks power.
s: Turtle symbol and reduced engine power (Volvo XC90 T8)
Functions of modules on Bus D unavailable
Lost-communication codes stored alongside
c: Control module software misjudging Bus D (Volvo XC90 T8: ECM update)
Supply or ground fault at a module on Bus D
Damaged wiring or loose connector on Bus D

U0056.d: U0056 says Vehicle Communication Bus D works, but its traffic is disturbed. Bentley documents it for the Continental GT (2018-20), GTC (2019-20) and Flying Spur (2020): U005600 with symptom numbers 12689537, 12689541 or 12689542 lands in the chassis control unit (address 0074) or in roll control systems 1 and 2 (00D4, 00D5).
s: Red or yellow suspension warning lamp (Bentley)
Dynamic ride fault message, several suspension codes stored
Functions drop out briefly and return
c: Chassis control software level prone to Bus D errors (Bentley)
Loose or dirty connector at a module on Bus D
Damaged harness between the modules on Bus D
A module on Bus D restarting because of weak supply

U0057.d: U0057 indicates an interrupted (+) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus D. Where Bus D is a two-wire CAN, such as the private chassis CAN Bentley files under that name, it is CAN-High.
s: Modules beyond the break unreachable
Sporadic errors among the remaining modules
c: (+) wire of Bus D broken where the harness flexes
Connector left unplugged or not latched after a repair

U0058.d: U0058 reports the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus D shorted to ground. If Bus D is a high-speed-style CAN, that conductor is CAN-High, and NXP's TJA1041 application note puts this short on the list of failures that stop communication completely.
s: All functions on Bus D fail together
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the modules involved
c: (+) wire of Bus D chafed through to ground
Harness pinched by a bracket or fastener
Shorted transceiver in a module on Bus D

U0059.d: U0059 means the (+) line of Vehicle Communication Bus D sits at too high a voltage, typically from contact with a battery or 5 V feed. On a high-speed CAN layout the line concerned is CAN-High, and the fault belongs to the shorts NXP calls hidden: communication goes on, and only a transceiver with bus diagnosis can report it.
s: Usually no symptom, code found during a scan
Occasional single warning from a module on Bus D
c: (+) wire of Bus D touching a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector bridging the bus wire to supply
Aftermarket device tapped into the bus wire

U0060.d: U0060 stands for a break in the (-) line of Vehicle Communication Bus D, CAN-Low on a two-wire CAN such as Bentley's private chassis network. Nodes cut off by the break still see CAN-High move, but a high-speed receiver judges only the voltage difference between both wires, so frames from the other side become unreadable to them.
s: Functions of modules beyond the break fail
Lost-communication codes for individual modules on Bus D
c: (-) wire of Bus D broken in the harness
Connector not fully latched after work on the vehicle

U0061.d: U0061 reports the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus D held at ground potential; a Bus D designed as high-speed CAN has CAN-Low in that role, which normally swings only between about 2.5 V and 1.5 V. Texas Instruments gives the tolerated common-mode range of ISO 11898 receivers as anything between -2 V and +7 V, so a grounded CAN-Low still lies inside the window and the receivers keep decoding; onsemi confirms tha
s: Often no symptom, code stored in a single module
Occasional interference-related message errors
c: (-) wire of Bus D chafed against a ground point or body edge
Water in a connector linking CAN-Low to a ground pin
Faulty transceiver pulling the (-) line down

U0062.d: U0062 means the (-) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus D is forced high, usually by contact with battery plus. Built as high-speed CAN, Bus D carries this fault on CAN-Low, which can then no longer be pulled down any more; onsemi and NXP both list this short among those under which no frame gets through, so every Bus D member eventually ends up bus-off and other networks log its absence.
s: All functions on Bus D fail together
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the modules involved
c: (-) wire of Bus D chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector linking the (-) wire to a supply pin
Termination or transceiver damaged by a lasting short to supply

U0063.d: U0063 covers a short circuit between both conductors of Vehicle Communication Bus D. On a CAN-type Bus D the receivers then measure no voltage difference, read every bit as recessive and cannot see any frame start; onsemi lists this short with those that block transmission completely.
s: All modules on Bus D unreachable at once
Several warning lamps or fallback modes
c: Harness crushed so that both Bus D wires touch
Water in a splice or connector bridging the pair
Damaged transceiver shorting its two bus pins

U0064.d: U0064 is the umbrella fault for Vehicle Communication Bus E, the fifth freely assignable network slot. Jaguar Land Rover documents it for the 2022-25 Range Rover (L460) and 2023-25 Range Rover Sport (L461): modules store U0064-88 (bus off) and U0064-87 (missing message), often together with U0080 codes for Bus F, when connector CM32B3/4 between the main body and instrument panel harnesses is not fully latched.
s: Electrical faults that come and go with cabin movement or temperature (JLR)
Modules on Bus E not responding, bus-off or missing-message entries
Codes for further networks stored alongside
c: Harness connector between body and instrument panel not fully latched (JLR CM32B3/4)
Bent or spread pins in that connector
Supply or ground fault at a module on Bus E

U0065.d: U0065 reports that Vehicle Communication Bus E is present but its communication is unreliable. In Audi and Volkswagen gateways this slot stands for the infotainment CAN.
s: Infotainment cannot be switched on or operated, screen sporadically blank (Audi A3)
Instrument cluster reports restricted functions
Stored only as a passive entry after a software update
c: Contact carrier not seated in the infotainment unit's quad-lock connector (Audi A3)
Brief dropout of the infotainment unit during a software update (VW Golf)
Loose or corroded terminals on Bus E

U0066.d: U0066 indicates a break in the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus E. Where Bus E is a two-wire CAN, like the infotainment CAN Audi and Volkswagen monitor under that slot, the (+) wire is CAN-High.
s: Modules beyond the break, often infotainment units, unreachable
Lost-communication codes for individual modules
c: (+) wire of Bus E broken in the harness
Contact carrier or terminal not seated in a multi-pin connector
Connector left unplugged after a repair

U0067.d: U0067 tells of the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus E being grounded. For a Bus E built as a high-speed CAN that is CAN-High, which a dominant bit needs to raise by about a volt; grounded, it cannot.
s: All functions on Bus E fail together (high-speed type)
Missing-message codes in modules on other networks
c: (+) wire of Bus E chafed through to body ground
Harness trapped behind the dashboard or a trim panel
Shorted transceiver in a module on Bus E

U0068.d: U0068 flags the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus E at an excessive voltage, from battery or a 5 V rail. If Bus E is a high-speed CAN, the line in question is CAN-High, and traffic continues: onsemi saw frames pass with altered dominant levels, NXP files the case under hidden failures.
s: Usually no symptom, code found by chance
Code stored in only one module on Bus E
c: (+) wire of Bus E chafed against a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector bridging the bus wire to supply
Aftermarket device connected to the bus wire

U0069.d: U0069 concerns a severed (-) line on Vehicle Communication Bus E, CAN-Low where Bus E is a CAN such as the infotainment CAN Volkswagen Group gateways supervise. Beyond splitting the network, the break matters for signal quality: Texas Instruments points out that stubs on a high-speed CAN are unterminated and should stay short, around 0.3 m, because reflections in them must die out ahead of the sampling point.
s: Modules beyond the break unreachable
Sporadic message errors among the remaining modules
c: (-) wire of Bus E broken in the harness
Connector not fully latched, contacts lifting
Terminal backed out of its housing

U0070.d: U0070 points to a (-) line of Vehicle Communication Bus E with a path to ground, CAN-Low wherever Bus E is a high-speed CAN. Traffic survives the short, which onsemi and NXP both confirm, so drivers rarely notice anything; onsemi traced a higher node current, because the upper driver stage now pushes current through the 60-ohm termination into ground.
s: Usually no symptom, code found during a scan
Occasional interference with audio or display functions on Bus E
c: (-) wire of Bus E chafed against body ground
Harness pinched during installation of trim or accessories
Faulty transceiver pulling CAN-Low to ground

U0071.d: With U0071 the (-) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus E sits too high, mostly by a short to battery voltage. Where Bus E is a high-speed CAN this is CAN-Low, and the bus dies: the line can no longer be pulled down, onsemi's node failed every start of frame, and NXP's TJA1041 note lists CAN-Low at battery or at 5 V as faults that prevent any communication.
s: All functions on Bus E fail together (high-speed type)
Gateway or other modules report lost communication
c: (-) wire of Bus E chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector linking the (-) wire to a supply pin
Damaged transceiver driving the (-) line high

U0072.d: U0072 describes the (-) and (+) wires of Vehicle Communication Bus E touching each other. On a high-speed CAN this ends communication: with the pair bridged there is no differential voltage, onsemi found transmission impossible, and NXP's TJA1041 note lists the short with the faults its bus diagnosis cannot detect.
s: All modules on Bus E unreachable (high-speed type)
Several warning messages, gateway reports lost communication
c: Harness crushed so that both Bus E wires touch
Water in a splice or connector bridging the pair
Damaged module input shorting its bus pins

U0073.d: U0073 is logged by a module whose own CAN controller has withdrawn from Bus A. Each failed transmission adds eight to its transmit error counter; above 255 the chip goes bus off and may rejoin only after 128 runs of 11 recessive bits (onsemi).
s: MIL and several cluster warnings at the same time
Transmission stuck in one gear or shifting harshly
Gauges fluctuate or drop out briefly
Lost-communication codes such as U0100 or U0101 in other modules
c: Bus A wires chafed through or shorted to ground in the harness
Loose or corroded ground point of a module on Bus A
Backed-out or loose terminals, e.g. in the transmission connector

U0074.d: U0074 tells that a module dropped into bus off on Bus B, which the makers that use it assign to an extra powertrain network. GM's 2019 ECM tables call it the Powertrain Expansion CAN, and the LT5 injection module rates its Bus B check Type B, two trips.
s: Service Engine Soon lamp or MIL on
Fuel pressure well above the requested value (GM trucks)
Shifter binds or shift concerns
No crank or start-stop inoperative
c: Damaged or poorly routed powertrain harness on Bus B
Engine module software fault, fixed by reprogramming
Loose connector, bent pin or badly seated fuse on a Bus B module

U0075.d: Which traffic runs on Bus C differs from brand to brand, so U0075 means little until the storing module is known. On the 2015 Cadillac Escalade with Driver Assist, the active safety module records it alongside radar and camera codes; GM found that a worn diagnostic interface or cable on DLC pins 3 and 11, where the object detection network ends, can create these entries falsely.
s: Service messages for steering, stability control or airbag
Driver assistance, radar or front camera unavailable
MIL on with no driveability complaint (FCA)
c: Bus C wires chafed on a seat frame or body edge
Engine module software setting the code falsely
Defective diagnostic interface or cable creating false entries

U0076.d: GM is the main public user of U0076. In the 2019 tables for the Corvette LT5 engine, Bus D is the Powertrain Sensor CAN, a private link between the ECM and engine-side devices.
s: Service Engine Soon lamp or MIL on
Fuel gauge erratic or wrong
Message counter codes stored alongside
c: ECM harness rubbing through on its bracket
Poor contact at a connector of the engine-side sensor bus
Faulty CAN transceiver inside the ECM

U0077.d: At GM, Bus E is usually a chassis-side network. In the 2018 tables for the LYX engine variant, the ECM watches it the same way as Bus A, more than five bus-off events within 0.81 s, but rates the result Type X without MIL; the transmission's default-to-park checks stay disabled while U0077 is set.
s: Service ABS, StabiliTrak or power steering messages
Suspension or all-wheel-drive warnings
Heavy steering when the steering module drops off
c: Corroded underbody connector in the Bus E harness
High resistance in the communication enable (wake-up) circuit
One-off software event in a module, cleared without repair

U0078.d: At GM the bus behind U0078 is often the single-wire low-speed GMLAN that ties body modules together. Equinox and Terrain models from 2010 to 2015 set it with lost-communication codes for body module, cluster and liftgate when water corrodes connector X901 above the liftgate glass.
s: Interior lamps or liftgate inoperative
Radio, climate panel or cluster go blank
Intermittent no-crank
c: Water intrusion and corrosion in a body harness connector
Low-speed bus wire pinched behind trim or headliner
Poor ground of the body control module

U0079.d: No manufacturer documents U0079 publicly, so what Bus G is depends entirely on the vehicle. The code belongs to the bus-off family: the controller of the reporting module has collected enough transmit errors to stop sending in order to protect the other nodes.
s: Functions of the reporting module unavailable
Lost-communication codes in other modules
c: Short between the Bus G wires or to ground
Faulty transceiver in the reporting module
Supply or ground dropouts at the reporting module

U007A.d: Bus H appears in no public manufacturer document for U007A; the code merely says that one module's CAN controller has switched to bus off on the network its maker labels H. A sensible check order follows from the physics.
s: Functions on Bus H fail or work only intermittently
Warning messages from several systems
c: Terminating resistor open or a terminating module disconnected

U007B.d: U007B is tied to no published manufacturer use; a Bus I only exists on vehicles split into many separate networks. The cause need not sit in the wiring at all.
s: Only the reporting module's functions drop out
Code returns soon after clearing
c: Transceiver in the reporting module unable to drive the bus
Weak supply or ground at the reporting module
Short or open in the Bus I wiring

U007C.d: For U007C no manufacturer publishes a use; a Bus J only exists where the electrical architecture splits the vehicle into ten or more CAN segments. Bus off is self-healing by design: once the controller has seen 128 sequences of 11 recessive bits it may rejoin, as onsemi explains, and the error counters start again from zero.
s: Stored history code without a current complaint
Brief, self-clearing dropouts of single functions
c: Loose pin or connector on Bus J opening briefly
Harness chafe causing brief shorts on Bus J

U007D.d: U007D is one of the few late-alphabet bus-off codes with a public trace, all from GM's 2017 full-size trucks and SUVs (Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon, Escalade). There a serial data gateway module connects many CAN segments, and PIT5586 lists U007D next to U0073, U0078 and a long row of lost-communication codes.
s: Instrument cluster gauges dead or fluctuating
No crank, no start or stall after starting
Radio, climate controls or steering wheel buttons inoperative
Numerous lost-communication codes in many modules
c: Bent, backed-out or loose terminals at the gateway connectors
Gateway microcontroller locks up and stops communicating

U007E.d: There is no public manufacturer documentation for U007E; the letter L is reserved for vehicles with a dozen or more networks. The code marks the last step of the CAN error ladder.
s: Single comfort or assistance function missing
Partner modules report lost communication
c: Persistent short or bad contact on Bus L
Fault inside the reporting module's CAN interface

U007F.d: U007F closes the range of bus-off codes that SAE runs from U0073 for Bus A to Bus M; the next code, U0080, already belongs to the general Bus F faults. No manufacturer publishes a use, and which physical network carries the letter M has to be read from the maker's service data.
s: Functions of the storing module unavailable
Several warning messages or none, depending on the module
c: A node unable to drive the bus, e.g. defective transceiver
Poor supply, ground or connector contact at the storing module

U0080.d: U0080 is the general fault of Vehicle Communication Bus F, and makers give that letter very different networks. In the 2019 Audi A6 and A7 3.0 TFSI the transmission module stores U008000 (Bus F) when its harness chafes on the crossmember or the FlexRay feed rubs on a module bracket, together with parking lock codes P17F4-P17F6 and U010100 in the engine module.
s: Transmission or other warning messages in the cluster
Stored code without any noticeable fault
Telematics or app services report errors
c: Bus F wiring chafed on a crossmember or bracket
Inline connector of Bus F not fully latched
Module on Bus F starts communicating too late after wake-up (stored code only)
Supply or ground fault of a Bus F module

U0081.d: U0081 marks Vehicle Communication Bus F as working but unreliable: frames arrive damaged, late or not at all from time to time, while the network as a whole stays up. No manufacturer documents U0081 publicly.
s: Functions on Bus F drop out briefly and return
Several modules store communication codes at the same time
c: Loose or corroded contact in a Bus F connector
Twisted pair of Bus F damaged or untwisted near a repair
Electrical interference from an aftermarket device
Module software that handles bus timing incorrectly

U0082.d: U0082 reports an interrupted (+) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus F. Where Bus F is FlexRay, as Audi's A6/A7 bulletin suggests, this is bus plus (BP); in a CAN it would be CAN-High.
s: Modules on the far side of the break no longer respond
Warnings that come and go with vehicle movement
c: (+) wire of Bus F broken at a flex point or after chafing
Terminal of the (+) wire pushed back in a connector
Inline connector of Bus F not fully latched

U0083.d: U0083 means the (+) line of Vehicle Communication Bus F is held too low, normally by a short to ground. On FlexRay, which Audi links to Bus F, the line is bus plus (BP).
s: Several functions on Bus F fail at once
Many lost-communication codes in other modules
c: (+) wire of Bus F chafed through to body metal
Harness pinched by a trim panel or bracket
Faulty transceiver pulling the (+) line to ground

U0084.d: U0084 is set when the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus F carries too much voltage, typically after contact with battery power. For a FlexRay Bus F, as in Audi's A6/A7, the wire is bus plus (BP); NXP rates the bus pins of its TJA1081B to withstand shorts to 14, 24 and 48 V and caps the output current at about 72 mA, so the hardware usually survives while signal levels are wrong.
s: Often no symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts of functions on Bus F
c: (+) wire of Bus F touching a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector bridging the bus to a supply pin
Faulty aftermarket wiring tapped into the bus

U0085.d: U0085 points to a severed (-) conductor on Vehicle Communication Bus F, that is bus minus (BM) where Bus F is FlexRay, as in the Audi A6/A7, or CAN-Low in a CAN. How hard the break hits depends on the topology.
s: Individual modules on Bus F stop responding
Code present with little or no effect when a second channel takes over
c: (-) wire of Bus F broken after chafing or repeated flexing
Spread or corroded terminal of the (-) wire
Poor earlier repair splice in the bus pair

U0086.d: U0086 says the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus F sits too low, usually shorted to ground. On a FlexRay Bus F, as in the Audi A6/A7, that wire is bus minus (BM).
s: Modules on Bus F fail to wake or drop out
On CAN layouts often no noticeable symptom
c: (-) wire of Bus F chafed against body metal
Harness trapped under a seat rail or trim
Transceiver of one module pulling the (-) line to ground

U0087.d: U0087 stands for a (-) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus F pulled too high, most often through contact with battery voltage. If Bus F is the FlexRay of an Audi A6/A7, the wire is bus minus (BM); held above BP, it creates a constant negative difference that receivers treat as DATA_0, so the channel looks permanently busy and no node can place a frame.
s: All functions on Bus F fail together
Warning lamps and messages from several systems
c: (-) wire of Bus F shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Moisture in a connector linking the (-) pin to a supply
Internally shorted transceiver in one module

U0088.d: With U0088 the two conductors of Vehicle Communication Bus F are bridged to each other. Signalling on both FlexRay and CAN rests on the difference between the wires, so with them joined there is none: a FlexRay receiver such as NXP's TJA1081B sees a difference below its activity threshold and treats the line as idle, while every sending node reads back something other than what it transmits and sets its bus error fla
s: Complete loss of the functions served by Bus F
Lost-communication codes for several modules
c: Bus F pair crushed so both wires touch
Water or corrosion bridging both wires in a splice or connector
Transceiver with an internal short between its bus pins

U0089.d: U0089 covers Vehicle Communication Bus G as a whole, the seventh of the network letters that SAE leaves for manufacturers to assign. No manufacturer documents U0089 publicly, and neither a service bulletin nor an OBD table names a network for the letter G, so the bus behind it can only be identified from the service information for the specific car.
s: Functions handled by Bus G modules fail or act erratically
Several modules hold communication codes
c: Damaged wiring or connector on Bus G
Supply or ground fault of a module on Bus G
Internal fault of a module disturbing the bus

U008A.d: U008A means Vehicle Communication Bus G still carries traffic, but not cleanly. No manufacturer documents U008A publicly.
s: Short dropouts of functions on Bus G
Messages that appear briefly and vanish
c: Aftermarket device tapped into Bus G with a long branch
Loose or corroded contact in a Bus G connector
Termination of Bus G missing or out of tolerance

U008B.d: On Vehicle Communication Bus G, U008B flags an open (+) conductor, which on a CAN means CAN-High. No manufacturer documents U008B publicly.
s: Some modules on Bus G not reachable with a scan tool
Intermittent faults that change with temperature or movement
c: (+) wire of Bus G broken at a hinge, seat or door passage
Terminal of the (+) wire pushed out of its connector cavity

U008C.d: U008C indicates a (+) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus G pulled too low, usually grounded. No manufacturer documents U008C publicly.
s: All modules on Bus G drop out together
Many warnings and lost-communication codes at once
c: (+) wire of Bus G chafed against body metal
Harness pinched by a screw, panel or seat
Defective transceiver holding CAN-High to ground

U008D.d: U008D is stored when the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus G carries excessive voltage, from a short to battery or another supply. No manufacturer documents U008D publicly.
s: Often no symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts on Bus G after a wiring fault
c: (+) wire of Bus G touching a battery or 24 V feed
Water in a connector linking the bus to a supply pin
Terminating resistor damaged by an earlier short

U008E.d: With U008E the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus G is open, CAN-Low where Bus G is a CAN. U008E is not documented publicly by any maker.
s: Modules beyond the break respond only sometimes
Code comes and goes with temperature or road shocks
c: (-) wire of Bus G broken at a flex point
Bus G connector not fully latched or a terminal backed out

U008F.d: U008F is the low-voltage fault on the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus G, which on a CAN means CAN-Low touching ground. No public manufacturer document uses U008F.
s: Often no noticeable effect, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts on Bus G
c: (-) wire chafed through to the body or a bracket
Moisture in a connector bridging the (-) pin to a ground pin
Damaged transceiver in one module pulling the line down

U0090.d: U0090 is logged when Bus G's (-) wire is pulled up, typically by a short to a supply feed; in CAN terms this is the CAN-Low line. U0090 is not described in any public manufacturer source.
s: All modules on Bus G stop responding at once
Warning lamps and lost-communication codes in several systems
Fault may come and go with the ignition switch position
c: (-) wire touching a switched ignition feed in the harness
(-) wire shorted to a permanent battery feed
Retrofitted equipment spliced into the bus wires

U0091.d: U0091 closes the Bus G block: the (-) and (+) wires of Vehicle Communication Bus G are joined, on a CAN CAN-Low to CAN-High. No manufacturer has published a use of U0091.
s: Complete loss of the functions served by Bus G
Scan tool cannot reach any module on Bus G
c: Bus wires crushed together, e.g. under a seat rail or panel
Corroded or wet splice bridging both wires
Internal short in one module's transceiver

U0092.d: U0092 stands for Vehicle Communication Bus H as a whole, the eighth network letter in SAE's list. Which network a carmaker files under H is not stated in any public bulletin or OBD table, and no manufacturer documents U0092 itself; the service data of the specific model has to tell.
s: Several functions handled by Bus H modules fail together
Problems worse at cranking or with a low battery
c: Weak battery or voltage drop so modules fall off the bus
Blown main fuse or bad feed supplying several Bus H modules
Wiring or connector fault on Bus H

U0093.d: U0093 says Vehicle Communication Bus H works, but with too many errors or too much delay. U0093 appears in no public manufacturer document.
s: Functions on Bus H drop out briefly and recover
Modules restart or freeze sporadically
c: Loose or corroded ground point of a Bus H module
Interference coupled in from nearby loads or retrofitted devices

U0094.d: U0094 reports that the (+) wire of Bus H is interrupted, CAN-High where Bus H is a CAN. No manufacturer documents U0094 publicly.
s: Single modules on Bus H not reachable
Fault appears intermittently or with movement
c: Broken (+) wire, e.g. at a hinge or flexing harness section
Terminal pushed out of a connector

U0095.d: U0095 indicates that the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus H is held too low, usually through a ground short (CAN-High on a CAN). No public manufacturer document uses U0095.
s: On high-speed CAN: all Bus H modules fail together
On fault-tolerant CAN: little or no noticeable effect
c: Harness pinched during a repair or installation
Faulty transceiver holding the (+) line low

U0096.d: U0096 is set once excessive voltage appears on the Bus H (+) wire, as from a short to battery or to the module supply; on a CAN this is CAN-High. U0096 is not documented by any manufacturer in public.
s: Often no symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts on Bus H
c: Water in a connector bridging the (+) pin to a supply pin
Faulty transceiver driving the (+) line high

U0097.d: U0097 points to an open (-) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus H, CAN-Low if Bus H is a CAN. The code is absent from public manufacturer documents.
s: Modules beyond the break respond only sometimes
Code with little effect on fault-tolerant layouts
c: Spread or bent terminal losing contact
Poor earlier repair or splice in the (-) wire

U0098.d: U0098 is stored once the Bus H (-) wire, CAN-Low on a CAN, sits too low, normally from a short to ground. No manufacturer has made a use of U0098 public.
s: Usually no noticeable symptom
Occasional errors on Bus H in electrically noisy conditions
c: Harness pinched by a fastener or panel
Faulty transceiver pulling the (-) line to ground

U0099.d: U0099 describes a (-) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus H held at too high a voltage, most often through contact with battery power; on a CAN that wire is CAN-Low. Nothing public from a manufacturer covers U0099.
s: On high-speed CAN: Bus H goes silent
On fault-tolerant CAN: degraded but working communication
c: (-) wire shorted to a battery feed
Corrosion or water in a connector between (-) and a supply pin
Faulty transceiver driving the (-) line high

U009A.d: U009A means the two wires of Vehicle Communication Bus H touch each other, on a CAN CAN-Low against CAN-High. No manufacturer documentation of U009A is public.
s: On high-speed CAN: complete loss of Bus H functions
Lost-communication codes for several modules
c: Wet or corroded splice joining both wires
Internal short in a module's transceiver

U009B.d: U009B addresses Vehicle Communication Bus I overall, the ninth network letter. Which network sits behind I is left to the manufacturer and not named in any public bulletin; U009B itself is not documented publicly by any maker.
s: Functions of Bus I modules fail or act erratically
Lost-communication codes in several modules
c: Open or shorted wire on Bus I
One module holding the bus dominant
Missing supply or ground at a Bus I module

U009C.d: U009C reports that Vehicle Communication Bus I carries traffic, but not at the quality the module expects. U009C has not been documented in public by any manufacturer.
s: Brief dropouts of functions on Bus I
Delayed reactions of displays or controls
c: Repair with untwisted or overly long wire

U009D.d: U009D covers Vehicle Communication Bus J in general, the tenth letter, and like I it has only this code and a performance code in the list, so open or shorted lines also end up here. No public bulletin names the network behind J, and no manufacturer documents U009D publicly.
s: Functions of Bus J modules missing after start
